(p-247) The Surah of the Children of Israel is Meccan, though it is said that the verse ﴿And indeed they almost tempted you﴾ up to the end of eight verses is Medinan. It has one hundred and eleven verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾. *Subhan* (glorification, or "Glory be to") is a noun meaning *tasbih* (glorification), which is *tanzih* (declaring Allah free of imperfection). It may also be used as a proper name for Allah, in which case it is detached from its genitive construction and not declined. The poet said:

*Indeed I said, when his boasting came to me: "Glory be to the one who is from ʿAlqama the boaster."*

Its accusative case is governed by a verb that is omitted and need not be stated. Opening the speech with it serves to declare Allah free from inability to do what is mentioned afterwards. *Asra* and *sara* have the same meaning. *Layla* is in the accusative as an adverb of time. Its indefiniteness indicates that the duration of the night journey was short, and for this reason it is read as *min al-layl* (during part of the night), meaning part of it, as in His saying: ﴿And during part of the night, rise for prayer with it﴾.

﴿from the Sacred Mosque﴾ refers to the specific Sacred Mosque, because it is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "While I was in the Sacred Mosque, in al-Hijr beside the House, between sleep and wakefulness, Gabriel came to me with al-Buraq."

Alternatively, it means from the Sacred Precinct (*al-haram*), and He called it the Sacred Mosque because the whole of it is a mosque, or because it encompasses the mosque, or so that the starting point and the end point correspond. This is based on the report that the Prophet (ﷺ) was sleeping in the house of Umm Hani after the night prayer, when he was taken on the night journey and returned during the same night. He recounted the story to her and said: "The prophets, peace be upon them, were presented to me, and I prayed with them." Then he went out to the Sacred Mosque and informed the Quraysh of it, and they were astonished at it, deeming it impossible. Some of those who had believed in him apostatised. Some men went to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "If he said it, then he has spoken the truth." He replied: "Do you ask me whether he is truthful about it?" They said: "Do you believe him about that?" He said: "Indeed I believe him about what is even more distant than that." For this he was named *al-Siddiq* (the Truthful). A group who had travelled to Bayt al-Maqdis asked him to describe it, so it was revealed to him and he began to look at it and describe it to them. They said: "As for the description, he has hit the mark." They said: "Tell us about our caravan." So he informed them of the number of its camels and their conditions, and said: "It will arrive on such-and-such a day at sunrise, led by a grey camel." They set out running toward the pass (*al-thaniyya*) and found the caravan just as he had said. Even so, they did not believe and said: ﴿This is nothing but evident magic﴾. This happened one year before the Hijra.

It is disputed whether it occurred in a dream or while awake, and whether it was in spirit or in body. The majority hold that he was taken bodily to Bayt al-Maqdis, and then ascended through the heavens until he reached Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary). For this reason the Quraysh were astonished and deemed it impossible. The claim of impossibility is refuted by what has been established in geometry (*al-handasa*): the distance between the two edges of the disk of the sun is twice the distance between the two edges of the globe of the earth, more than one hundred and sixty times. Moreover, its lower edge reaches the position of its upper edge in less than a second. It has also been demonstrated in theology (*al-kalam*) that bodies are equal in receiving accidents (*al-aʿrad*, contingent attributes), and that Allah is able over all possibilities (*al-mumkinat*). So He is able to create such swift motion in the body of the Prophet (ﷺ), or in what carries him. Astonishment is among the necessary consequences of miracles.

﴿to the Farthest Mosque﴾, which is Bayt al-Maqdis, because at that time there was no mosque beyond it. ﴿whose surroundings We have blessed﴾ with the blessings of religion and of worldly life, because it is the place of descent of revelation and the place of worship of the prophets, peace be upon them, from the time of Musa, peace be upon him, and it is surrounded by rivers and trees. ﴿That We might show him of Our signs﴾ (p-248) such as his going in a portion of the night a distance of a month's journey, his witnessing Bayt al-Maqdis, the prophets, peace be upon them, appearing to him, and his standing in their stations. The shift in speech from the third person to the first person (*al-taknim*) serves to magnify those blessings and signs. It is also read *liyuriyahu* with the letter *ya*.

﴿Indeed He is the All-Hearing﴾ of the words of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿the All-Seeing﴾ of his deeds, so He honours him and brings him near according to that.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 17, verses 2–3:

﴿And We gave Moses the Book and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel, [saying]: "Do not take﴾ (*an lā tattakhidhū*) [here *an* is the interpretive particle], as in your saying: "I wrote to you that I should do such-and-such." Abu 'Amr read *an lā yattakhidhū* with the *yāʾ* (third person, "that they not take"). ﴿besides Me as a trustee﴾, meaning a lord to whom you entrust your affairs, other than Me.

﴿The offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾ is in the accusative, either by *ikhtiṣāṣ* (specification, singling out) or by *nidāʾ* (direct address, vocative), if *an lā tattakhidhū* is read with the *tāʾ* as a prohibition (*nahy*). The meaning is: We said to them, "Do not take besides Me a trustee." Or it is one of the two objects of *lā tattakhidhū*, with ﴿besides Me﴾ as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) of ﴿a trustee﴾. This is like His saying: ﴿nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords﴾. It is also read in the nominative, either as the predicate of an omitted subject (*khabar mubtadaʾ maḥdhūf*) or as an apposition (*badal*) from the *wāw* of *tattakhidhū*. The word *dhurriyyata* is read with a *kasra* on the *dhāl*. In this there is a reminder of God Most High's blessings upon them in saving their fathers from drowning by carrying them with Noah, peace be upon him, in the ship.

﴿Indeed he﴾, meaning Noah, peace be upon him, ﴿was a grateful servant﴾, who praises God Most High in all his circumstances. In this there is an indication that his deliverance and that of those with him was by the blessing of his gratitude, and an exhortation to his offspring to follow his example. It is also said that the pronoun refers to Moses, peace be upon him.

**Verses 4–5 (al-Baydawi's commentary)**

﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel﴾: And We revealed to them a revelation that is decisive and definitive (muqtadiyan mabtutan). ﴿in the Book﴾: in the Torah (al-Tawrat). ﴿You will surely cause corruption on the earth﴾: this is the answer to an omitted oath, or the decree was made to take the place of an oath, given the definitive nature of the decree. ﴿twice﴾: two acts of corruption. The first was violating the rulings of the Torah and killing Shi'ya' (Isaiah), and it is said Armiya' (Jeremiah). The second was killing Zakariyya (Zechariah) and Yahya (John), and plotting to kill ʿIsa (Jesus), peace be upon them. ﴿And you will become exceedingly arrogant﴾: you will be arrogant toward the obedience of God Most High, or you will wrong the people.

﴿When the promise of the first of them came﴾: the promise of punishment for the first of them. ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours﴾: Bakhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar), the governor of Lahrasf over Babil (Babylon), and his troops. It is said that it was Jalut (Goliath) al-Jazari. It is also said that it was Sanharib (Sennacherib) from the people of Nineveh (Naynawa). ﴿possessing great might﴾: possessing strength and fierceness in war. ﴿So they went through﴾: they roamed searching for you. It is also read with the unpointed ha' (jahasu); the two forms are brothers in meaning. ﴿into the midst of the homes﴾: into the middle of them, for killing and raiding. They killed their elders, took their young captive, burned the Torah, and destroyed the Masjid (the Temple). The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school of theology), when they rejected God's empowering of the disbelieving king to do this, interpreted the "sending" as merely leaving them free and not preventing them. ﴿And it was a promise fulfilled﴾: the promise of their punishment was bound to be carried out.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 6:

﴿Then We gave you the return (of victory) over them﴾, that is, the dynasty and the triumph. ﴿Over them﴾, over those who were sent against you. This was by God placing in the heart of Bahman ibn Isfandiyar, when he inherited the kingship from his grandfather Kishtasp ibn Lohrasp, compassion for them. So he returned their captives to Syria and made Daniel (Daniyal) their ruler, and they prevailed over those who were there from the followers of Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar). Or it was by God empowering Dawud (David), upon him be peace, against Jalut (Goliath), and he killed him. ﴿And We aided you with wealth and sons, and made you more numerous in manpower﴾, compared to what you had been. The nafir (manpower) is the one who goes forth with a man from his people. It was also said that it is the plural of nafar, and they are the people gathered to go out against the enemy.

(p-249) ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves﴾, for its reward is for them. ﴿And if you do evil, it is against them﴾, for its consequence falls upon them. He mentioned "them" with the lam (la) for the sake of rhyme (izdiwaj). ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾: the promise of punishment of the last time. ﴿To sadden your faces﴾: that is, We sent them so that they would sadden your faces, meaning, so that they would make your faces show the marks of distress upon them; the object was omitted because its earlier mention indicates it. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and Abu Bakr read "liyasu'a" (in the singular), and the pronoun in it refers either to the promise, or to the sending, or to God. The reading of al-Kisa'i with the nun supports it. It was also read "linasu'anna" with the nun and the ya', with the nun both light and heavy (mukhaffafah and muthaqqalah), and "lanasu'anna" with a fatha on the lam, in all four ways, on the basis that it is the answer of "idha" (the conditional). The lam in His saying ﴿and that they might enter the Masjid﴾ is connected to an omitted element, which is "We sent them." ﴿As they entered it the first time, and that they might destroy﴾: that they might ruin. ﴿What they had conquered﴾: what they had overpowered and gained control over, or the duration of their dominance. ﴿With complete destruction﴾: this came about when God empowered the Persians over them a second time, and the king of Babylon from among the kings of the factions, named Judhurz, or it is said Hardus, invaded them. It is said that the commander of the army entered the place of their sacrifices and found in it blood boiling. He asked them about it, and they said: "It is the blood of an offering that was not accepted from us." He said: "You have not told me the truth," and he killed thousands of them over it, yet the blood did not settle. Then he said: "If you do not tell me the truth, I will not leave a single one of you." They said: "It is the blood of Yahya." He said: "For the like of this your Lord takes vengeance upon you." Then he said: "O Yahya, my Lord and your Lord knows what befell your people because of you. Be still, by God's leave, before I leave none of them alive." So it became still.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 8:

﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you﴾ after the last time. ﴿And if you return﴾ to a second instance, ﴿We will return﴾ a third time to your punishment, when they had returned to denying Muhammad (ﷺ) and intending to kill him. So God, exalted is He, returned by setting him (Muhammad, ﷺ) over them, and he killed the Qurayza and expelled the Banu al-Nadir, and imposed the jizya (poll tax) on the rest. This is for them in this world. ﴿And We have made Hell for the disbelievers a ḥaṣīr﴾, a prison from which they cannot be able to leave, forever and ever. It was also said it means a carpet, as a ḥaṣīr is spread out.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 9–10:

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright.﴾ (It guides) to the state or the way which is most upright of states or ways.

﴿And gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that for them is a great reward.﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿wa-yubashshiru﴾ (and gives good tidings) with the lighter form (yubshiru).

﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We have prepared for them a painful punishment.﴾ This is in conjunction with ﴿that for them is a great reward﴾, and the meaning is that it gives the believers good tidings with two kinds of glad tidings: their reward and the punishment of their enemies. Or it is in conjunction with ﴿yubashshiru﴾, with the implied verb "yukhbiru" (it informs).

And man prays for evil ﴿وَيَدْعُ الإنْسانُ بِالشَّرِّ﴾: he calls upon God, in his anger, for evil against himself, his family, or his wealth. Or he calls upon Him for something he thinks is good but which is in fact evil. ﴿دُعاءَهُ بِالخَيْرِ﴾: like his prayer for good. ﴿وَكانَ الإنْسانُ عَجُولا﴾: man hastens toward everything that occurs to his mind without considering its consequence. It has also been said that the intended meaning is Adam, peace be upon him, for when the spirit reached his navel he tried to stand up and fell.

It is narrated: "The Prophet, peace be upon him, handed a captive over to Sawda bint Zam'a, and she had mercy on him because of his groaning and loosened his bonds. He fled, and he (the Prophet) prayed against her, invoking the cutting off of her hand. Then he regretted it and said, peace be upon him: 'O Allah, I am only a human being. Whomever I curse, make my curse a mercy for him.' Then this was revealed."

It is also permissible that by man is meant the disbeliever, and by the prayer, his seeking to hasten the punishment mockingly, like the saying of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith: "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, give victory to the better of the two parties," and "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You..." (the verse). He was answered, and his neck was struck off in cold blood on the day of Badr. (p-250)

﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾ indicating the All-Powerful, the All-Wise, through their succession in a single fixed order, though it was possible for it to be otherwise.

﴿So We effaced the sign of the night﴾, i.e., the sign which is the night, by its darkness. The idafa (genitive construction) in both phrases is for specification (tabyin), like the idafa of a number to the thing counted.

﴿And We made the sign of the day [to be] seeing﴾: illuminating, or giving sight to the people, from "absarahu fa-basura" (he made him see, so he saw). Or it means "making its people see," as in the saying of the Arabs, "ajbana al-rajulu" (the man became cowardly) when his people were cowards. It has been said that the two signs are the moon and the sun. The sense of the sentence is: "And We made the two luminaries of the night and the day two signs," or "We made the night and the day possessors of two signs." The effacing of the sign of the night, which is the moon, is making it dark in itself, its light obliterated, or diminishing its light little by little until it reaches the crescent's disappearance (al-mihaq). And He made the sign of the day, which is the sun, "seeing," meaning He made it possessed of rays by which things are seen by its light.

﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾: that you may seek, in the brightness of the day, the means of your livelihood, and through it reach the clarification of your affairs.

﴿And that you may know﴾ by their difference or by their movements, ﴿the number of years and the reckoning﴾, and the kind of reckoning, ﴿and every thing﴾ that you need in matters of religion and worldly life. ﴿We have explained it with [full] explanation﴾: We have made it clear with an explanation free of ambiguity.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 13:

﴿And every person's omen We have fastened to his neck﴾: his deed and what has been decreed for him, as if it flew to him from the nest of the unseen and the nest of destiny. This is because they used to seek good omens and bad omens from the flight of birds and their movements to the right or left, so the term was borrowed for that which is the cause of good and evil, from the decree of God Most High and the action of the servant.

﴿around his neck﴾: like the binding of a collar around his neck. ﴿And We will bring forth for him on the Day of Resurrection a record﴾: it is the record of his deeds, or his soul imprinted with the traces of his deeds, for voluntary actions produce states in the soul, and therefore their repetition produces stable dispositions (malakat) in it. It is in the accusative either as an object or as a circumstantial state (hal) of an omitted object, which is the pronoun referring to the omen. This is supported by the reading of Ya'qub (﴿wayakhruju﴾) from kharaja, and "yukhraju" (it is brought forth), and it was also read "wayukhriju" (and He brings forth), meaning God, Mighty and Majestic is He. ﴿He will find it spread open﴾: to remove the covering. These two are attributes of the record, or ﴿yalqahu﴾ is an attribute and ﴿manshuran﴾ is a circumstantial state of its object. Ibn 'Amir read (﴿yulqahu﴾) in the passive form, from "laqitahu kadha" (I met him thus).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 14–15:

﴿Read your book.﴾ This is on the supposition of an implied saying (al-qawl al-muqaddar). ﴿Sufficient is your own self today to take account of you.﴾ That is, your own self suffices. The bāʾ (al-bāʾ al-zāʾidah, the superfluous bāʾ) is extra, and ﴿ḥasīban﴾ is a tamyīz (specification of the noun). ʿAlā is its complement (ṣilah), because the word is either in the sense of the one who reckons (al-ḥāsib), like al-ṣarīm in the sense of al-ṣārim and ḍarīb al-qidāḥ in the sense of its striker, from ḥasaba ʿalayhi kadhā (he reckoned such-and-such against him); or in the sense of the sufficient one (al-kāfī), and so it is placed in the position of the witness (al-shahīd), because it suffices the claimant for whatever concerns him. Its masculine form is used because reckoning and testimony are among the things that men undertake; or it is on the interpretation of "self" as "person."

﴿Whoever is guided, is only guided for his own self, and whoever goes astray, only goes astray to its own detriment.﴾ His guidance does not save another, and his misguidance does not destroy anyone other than himself. ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another.﴾ No soul carrying a burden shall carry the burden of another soul; rather, it carries only its own burden.

﴿And We never punish until We have sent a messenger.﴾ He (the messenger) makes the proofs clear and lays down the laws, so that he establishes the proof against them. In this is evidence that there is no obligation before revelation (sharʿ) [i.e., that obligations are not binding before the law is revealed].

﴿And when We intend to destroy a town﴾: when Our will becomes attached to destroying a people, in order to carry out Our previous decree, or when its appointed time has drawn near, as people say: when the sick man intends to die, his illness grows more severe. ﴿We command its affluent ones﴾: its wealthy who live in luxury, to obedience, through the tongue of a messenger (p-251) whom We sent to them. This is indicated by what precedes and what follows it, for dissoluteness (fisq) is departure from obedience and persistence in disobedience, so it indicates obedience by way of contrast (muqabalah). It has also been said: "We commanded them to dissoluteness," because of His saying: ﴿so they committed dissoluteness therein﴾, as in your saying, "I commanded him and he read (fa-qara')." From this, nothing is understood except the command to reading, while the command is a metaphor (majaz) for urging him to it, or for causing it, in that He poured upon them of blessings what made them insolent and led them to wickedness. It is also possible that it has no implied object, as in people's saying, "I commanded him and he disobeyed me." It has also been said that its meaning is "We increased them," as one says: "amartu al-shay'" and "amartuhu," and it becomes "umira" when you make it abundant. In the hadith: "The best wealth is a well-tended irrigation channel and a fruitful mare (muhrah ma'murah)," meaning one with many offspring. This too is a metaphor derived from the meaning of seeking. It is supported by the reading of Ya'qub, "amarna" (with a long vowel), and the transmission of ﴿amarna﴾ from Abu 'Amr. It is possible that it is derived from "umira" with a damma, meaning "amarah," i.e., We made them rulers (umara'). The specification of "affluent ones" is because others follow them, and because they are quicker to folly and more capable of wickedness. ﴿So the word came due against it﴾: meaning the word of punishment previously decreed, by its arrival, or by the manifestation of their sins, or by their immersion in sins. ﴿So We utterly destroyed it﴾: We annihilated it by destroying its people and ruining their dwellings.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 17–18:

﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah﴾. And many have We destroyed. ﴿Of the generations﴾ is an explanation for "you" and a specification of it (tamyiz). ﴿After Noah﴾, such as ʿAd and Thamud.

﴿And your Lord is sufficient as one who is All-Aware and All-Seeing of the sins of His servants﴾. He perceives their inner and outer aspects, and so He punishes them for them. The placing of "Khabir" (All-Aware) first is due to the precedence of what it relates to (its object).

﴿Whoever desires the hasty life﴾, his concern being confined to it. ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will, for whomever We desire﴾. He restricted what is hastened and the one for whom it is hastened by the will and the desire, because not every wisher finds what he wishes for, nor does everyone who has something obtain all that he desires; and so that it be known that the matter rests on the will, and that the aspiration is a bounty. (﴿for whomever We desire﴾) is a substitute (badal al-ba'ḍ, partial substitute) for "him". It has been read as "ma yashaʾu" (what He wills), with the pronoun referring to God Most High, so that it agrees with the well-known reading. It has also been said that "li-man" means that it is specific to those whom God Most High intends by it. It has also been said that the verse concerns the hypocrites who would show off to the Muslims and fight alongside them, while their aim was nothing but to share in the spoils and the like. ﴿Then We have made Hell for him; he will burn in it, censured and expelled﴾, driven away from the mercy of God Most High.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 19–20:

﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it﴾: its due striving, which is doing what He has commanded and refraining from what He has forbidden, not drawing near (to God) through what they invent by their own opinions. The benefit of the lam (in lahā, "for it") is to take intention and sincerity into account. ﴿And he is a believer﴾: a sound faith with no association (of partners with God) in it and no denial, for it is the foundation. ﴿Those﴾: those who combine the three conditions. ﴿Their striving will be appreciated﴾ by God, the Exalted, meaning accepted by Him and rewarded for it, for God's appreciation (shukr) is the reward for obedience.

﴿Each﴾: each one of the two groups. The tanwin (in kullan) is a substitute for the genitive noun that was added to (i.e., kullan replaces kulla farīq, "each group"). ﴿We extend﴾: with provision, time after time, and We make its latter (portion) an extension of its former. ﴿These and those﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿each﴾. ﴿From the provision of your Lord﴾: from His bestowed gift; min muʿṭāhu is connected to ﴿We extend﴾. ﴿And the provision of your Lord has never been restricted﴾: forbidden, not withheld in this world from believer or disbeliever, as an act of grace.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 21–22:

﴿Look how We have favoured some of them over others﴾ in provision. The accusative of ﴿how﴾ (kayfa) is governed by ﴿favoured﴾ (faddalna) as a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

(p-252) ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preference.﴾ That is, the disparity in the Hereafter is greater, because the disparity there is by way of Paradise and its degrees, and the Fire and its depths.

﴿Do not set up another god alongside Allah﴾. The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and what is meant by it is his community, or it is for everyone. ﴿Then you will sit⁠﴾ (fa-taqʿuda), that is, you will become, from their saying: "He sharpened the blade until it became (qaʿadat) like a spear," or you will become powerless (fa-taʿjiza), from their saying: "He sat (qaʿada) from the matter," meaning he became unable to do it. ﴿Reviled and forsaken﴾: gathering upon yourself blame from the angels and the believers, and abandonment from Allah the Exalted. Its implication is that the one who affirms the oneness of God (al-muwahhid) will be praised and aided.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 21–22:

﴿Look how We have favoured some of them over others﴾ in provision. The accusative of ﴿how﴾ (kayfa) is governed by ﴿favoured﴾ (faddalna) as a circumstantial qualifier (hal).

(p-252) ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preference.﴾ That is, the disparity in the Hereafter is greater, because the disparity there is by way of Paradise and its degrees, and the Fire and its depths.

﴿Do not set up another god alongside Allah﴾. The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and what is meant by it is his community, or it is for everyone. ﴿Then you will sit⁠﴾ (fa-taqʿuda), that is, you will become, from their saying: "He sharpened the blade until it became (qaʿadat) like a spear," or you will become powerless (fa-taʿjiza), from their saying: "He sat (qaʿada) from the matter," meaning he became unable to do it. ﴿Reviled and forsaken﴾: gathering upon yourself blame from the angels and the believers, and abandonment from Allah the Exalted. Its implication is that the one who affirms the oneness of God (al-muwahhid) will be praised and aided.

**"And your Lord has decreed"**: He has commanded a matter that is definitively settled. **"that you worship not"**: meaning, that you not worship. **"except Him"**: because the utmost degree of veneration is due only to One who possesses the utmost degree of greatness and the ultimate bounty. This is like a detailed explanation of the striving for the Hereafter. It is also permissible for أنْ (an, "that") to be explanatory (mufassira, *tafsiriyya*) and for لا (la) to be a prohibitive particle (nahiya). **"and to parents, kindness"**: meaning, and that you do good to them, or, "and be kind to your parents," because they are the apparent cause of your existence and sustenance. The preposition بِ (bi) may not be construed as attached to إحْسانًا (ihsanan, "kindness"), because its complement (silah) cannot precede the word it governs. **"Should either or both of them reach old age with you"**: إمّا (imma) is the conditional particle إنْ (in) with ما (ma) added to it for emphasis, and for this reason the emphatic nun (al-nun al-muakkida) may attach to the verb. أحَدُهُما (ahaduhuma, "either of them") is the subject (fa'il) of يَبْلُغَنَّ (yablughanna, "reach"). According to the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i, it is a substitute (badal) for the alif of يَبْلُغانِ (yablughan, "reach," dual) referring to الوالِدَيْنِ (al-walidayn, "the parents"). كِلاهُما (kilahuma, "both of them") is conjoined (ma'tuf) to أحَدُهُما, either as a subject or as a substitute. For this reason it is not permissible for it to be an emphasis (ta'kid) of the alif. The meaning of عِنْدَكَ (indaka, "with you") is that they are in your care and under your guardianship. **"then do not say to them, 'Uff'"**: then do not show annoyance at what is repulsive from them, and do not find their upkeep burdensome. أُفٍّ (uff) is a sound that indicates irritation. It is also said that it is the verbal noun (ism al-fi'l, *ism al-fi'l*) meaning "I am annoyed," and it is built on kasra because of the meeting of two quiescent letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn). Its tanwin (tanwin) in the reading of Nafi' and Hafs is for indefiniteness (tankir). Ibn Kathir, Ibn Amir and Ya'qub read it with fatha for lightening (takhfif). It was also read with tanwin and with damma for assimilation (ittiba'), like مُنْذُ (mundhu) read both with and without tanwin. The prohibition of this implies the prohibition of all other kinds of harm by way of a fortiori analogy (qiyas bi-tariq al-awla, *a fortiori*). It has also been said that it is by custom, as when you say, "So-and-so does not own a *naqir* or *qitmir*." For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade Hudhayfah from killing his father while he was in the ranks of the polytheists. He prohibited what harms them after commanding kindness to them. **"and do not scold them"**: and do not rebuke them for what does not please you, with harshness.

It has been said that النَّهْيُ (al-nahy, "forbidding"), النَّهْرُ (al-nahr, "scolding") and النَّهْمُ (al-nahm, "rebuking") are cognates. **"and speak to them"**: instead of the annoyance and scolding. **"a generous word"**: a good word, free of any harshness.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 24:

﴿And lower to them the wing of humility﴾ — humble yourself before them and be modest towards them. He made humility (dhull) to have a wing, just as Labid said in his verse:

❝And on a day of wind that has uncovered [everything], and cold, when the north wind has taken its reins in hand❞

He made the north wind a hand, or the cold a rein-holder. His command to lower [the wing] is an intensification, or he meant [the lowering of] his wing, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾. Its annexation to humility (dhull) serves to clarify and intensify, just as Hatim is annexed to generosity (jud), and the meaning is: lower to them your humble wing. It has been read as "adh-dhill" with a kasra, which is submission (al-inqiyad), and its adjective derived from it is dhalul. ﴿From mercy﴾ — out of the abundance of your mercy towards them, because they are in need of the one who was, in the past, the neediest of God's creation to them. ﴿And say: My Lord, have mercy on them﴾ — and call upon God, Exalted is He, to have mercy on them with His everlasting mercy, and do not rely on your mercy, which passes away, even if they are two unbelievers, because part of mercy is that you guide them. ﴿As they raised me when I was small﴾ — with a mercy like their mercy upon me, and their upbringing and guidance of me in my childhood, as a fulfilment of Your promise to those who show mercy.

It is narrated: "A man said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: Indeed my two parents have reached such old age that I attend to them with what they attended to me in childhood. Have I fulfilled their right? He said: No, for they used to do that while they loved your remaining alive, and you do that while you desire their death."

Your Lord knows best what is in your souls: the intention of kindness toward them both and the belief in the reverence that is due to them. This is a warning, as if to say: (lest you) conceal in yourselves aversion and distaste toward them. ﴿If you are righteous﴾, intending goodness. ﴿Then indeed He is ever forgiving to the ones who turn back in repentance﴾, to those who repeatedly turn back (to Him). ﴿Forgiving﴾ of what has proceeded from them at a moment of constriction of the breast, of harm or shortcoming. In this there is a great severity. It may also be that it is general for every penitent, and it includes the one who wrongs his parents and then repents of his wrong, since it follows directly upon it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 26–27:

﴿And give to the near of kin his due﴾ from the maintaining of ties of kinship (silat al-rahim), good companionship, and kindness toward them. Abu Hanifa said: their due, when they are mahram relatives and poor, is that one spend upon them. It has also been said that what is meant by "the near of kin" is the relatives of the Messenger ﷺ. ﴿And the needy and the wayfarer; and do not squander wastefully﴾ by spending wealth on what is not fitting and by expending it in a manner of extravagance (israf). The root of tabdhir (squandering) is dispersal.

It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said to Sa'd while he was performing ablution: "What is this extravagance?" He said: "Is there extravagance in ablution?" He said: "Yes, even if you were at a flowing river."

﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾ being like them in wickedness, for waste and destruction are evil; or [they are] their friends and followers, because they obey them in extravagance and in spending on acts of disobedience.

It is reported that they used to slaughter camels and gamble over them, and squander their wealth for the sake of reputation, so God forbade them from that and commanded them to spend in acts of devotion.

﴿And Satan has ever been to his Lord ungrateful﴾ exceeding in disbelief in Him, so he should not be obeyed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 28:

﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ — that is, if you turn away from the near of kin, the needy, and the wayfarer out of shame at having to refuse them. It is also possible that turning away from them is meant figuratively, as in not benefiting them (kināyah).

﴿seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for﴾ — that is, while awaiting provision from God which you hope will come to you so that you may give it to them, or while waiting for it. It has been said that the meaning is: for lack of provision from your Lord which you hope He will open up for you. The word ibtigha' (seeking) is placed in this position because it is the cause (musabbab) of that lack. It is also possible that it is connected to the answer, which is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then speak to them a gentle word﴾, meaning: then speak to them a gentle word, seeking the mercy of God through your mercy toward them by speaking to them kindly. Al-maysur ("ease, that which is easy") derives from the ease of a matter, like sa'ada al-rajul (the man prospered) and nahusa (he was unlucky). It has also been said that the "gentle word" (al-qawl al-maysur) is supplication for them for what is easy, which is ease itself, like "may God Most High make you rich" (aghnakumu Allah) and "may God provide for us and for you" (razaqana Allah wa-iyyakum).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 29–30:

﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it completely outstretched﴾. These are two metaphors for the withholding of the miser and the extravagance of the squanderer. He forbids both, commanding moderation between them, which is generosity (karam). ﴿So you will sit reproached﴾: you will become blameworthy in the sight of God and in the sight of people, because of extravagance and poor management. ﴿Destitute﴾: regretful, or left cut off, with nothing in your possession, from the exhaustion (hasrah) of the journey once it has reached its end.

And on the authority of Jabir: "While the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sitting, a boy came to him and said: 'My mother asks you to clothe her in a garment.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Come back to us from one time to another.' So he went to his mother, and she said: 'Tell him: My mother asks you for the garment you are wearing.' So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered his house, took off his shirt, gave it to him, and sat naked. Bilal called the adhan and they waited for him for the prayer, but he did not come out. Then God revealed that, and consoled him with His words: ﴿Indeed your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾, that is, He expands it and constricts it by His will, which follows perfect wisdom. So what burdens you of poverty is only for your own benefit."

﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing﴾: He knows their secrets and their open affairs, so He knows what is good for them that is hidden from them. It is possible that what is meant is that extending and withholding are both by the command of God the Exalted, who knows the inner and outer realities. As for the servants, they must be moderate. Or it means that He, the Exalted, extends at one time and withholds at another, so follow His way and do not withhold completely, nor extend completely, and that this serves as a preparation for His saying, the Exalted:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 31:

﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ — (for fear of destitution). Their killing their children was burying their daughters alive for fear of poverty. So He forbade them from it and guaranteed them their provision, saying: ﴿We provide for them and for you. Indeed, their killing is a great sin (khiti'an kabiran)﴾ — a great sin, because of what it entails of cutting off offspring and the termination of the kind. And ﴿khata'* (sin)﴾ means sin (al-ithm); it is said: khati'a khata'an, like atham ithman. Ibn 'Amir recited ﴿khata'an﴾, which is the noun of one who errs (akhta'a), opposite to right (al-sawab). It was also said that it is a dialect form of it, like mithl and mathal, and hidhr and hadhar. Ibn Kathir recited “khital'” with a long vowel and a kasra, and it is either a dialect form of it or the verbal noun of khata'a. Although it is not heard, it has come as takhata'a in his saying:

Takhata'ahu al-qannas hatta wajadtuhu... wa kharturuhu fi manqa'i al-ma'i rasibu

It is built upon this. It has also been read khata'an with a fatha and a long vowel, and khata with the hamza omitted, both with fatha and with kasra.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 32:

﴿And do not approach adultery (al-zina)﴾ by resolving upon it or by engaging in its preliminaries, let alone actually committing it. ﴿Indeed, it is an abomination (fahisha)﴾, an act whose ugliness is manifest and excessive. ﴿And evil is it as a way﴾, and wretched is it as a path, which is the seizing of women for intercourse, leading to the severing of lineages and the stirring up of strife.

And do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right. ﴿Except in one of three cases: disbelief after faith; fornication after being married (ihsan); and deliberately killing a believer who is protected.﴾ ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully﴾, not deserving to be killed. ﴿We have given his heir﴾, meaning the one who takes charge of his affairs after his death, namely the inheritor. ﴿Authority﴾, meaning a right to hold the killer accountable according to what killing requires, against whoever is liable for it, or to demand retaliation (qisas) against the killer. The words of God Most High ﴿wrongfully﴾ indicate that the killing was a deliberate act of aggression, since accidental killing is not called wrongful. ﴿So let him not commit excess﴾, meaning the killer, ﴿in killing﴾, by killing someone who does not deserve to be killed. A sensible person does not do what brings destruction upon himself, and the heir does not do so by mutilation, or by killing someone other than the killer. The first interpretation is supported by the recitation of Ubayy, "fa-la tusrifu" (plural). Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "fa-la tusrif" (singular), addressing one of the two. ﴿Indeed, he was supported﴾: the reason for the prohibition is given as a resumptive (istinaf) clause. The pronoun may refer to the one who was killed, for he is supported in this world by the establishment of retaliation for his killing, and in the Hereafter by reward. It may refer to his heir, for God Most High supported him by making retaliation obligatory for him and commanding the rulers to assist him. It may refer to the one whom the heir kills in excess, by requiring retaliation or discretionary punishment (ta'zir) beyond what is due. The burden falls upon the one who commits excess.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 34:

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾, [meaning] far less dispose of it. ﴿except in the way that is best﴾, except by the manner that is best.

﴿until he reaches his maturity﴾: this is a limit (ghayah) for the permissibility of disposal, which is indicated by the exception (istithna'). ﴿And fulfil the covenant﴾, [meaning] that which Allah has bound you to of His obligations, or that which you have bound yourselves to, or other than that. ﴿Indeed, the covenant was ever [that about which one will be] questioned﴾: it is demanded, one who makes the covenant being required not to waste it and to fulfil it; or it is "questioned about," so that the one who breaks it is asked and rebuked for it, "Why did you break it?"; or the covenant itself is questioned as a reproach to the one who breaks it, as is said to the buried infant girl, ﴿for what sin was she killed?﴾. In that case it is a figure of imagination (takhyil). It is also permissible to mean that the party to the covenant was the one who would be questioned.(p-255)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 35:

﴿And give full measure when you measure out﴾ and do not diminish it, ﴿and weigh with a true balance﴾, with a sound, upright scale. The word qistas (balance, scale) is Roman (Byzantine Greek) in origin but has been Arabicized, and this does not detract from the Arabic character of the Qur'an, because when the Arabs use a foreign word and treat it like their own speech in its inflection (i'rab), its definiteness and indefiniteness (ta'rif and tankir), and similar features, it becomes Arabic. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read the qaf with a kasra here and in [surah] al-Shu'ara'. ﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome (ta'wil)﴾: ahsan ta'wilan means ahsan 'aqibatan (more excellent in its consequence); ta'wil is on the pattern taf'il, from the verb a-la, meaning he returned.

﴿And do not pursue﴾: do not follow. It is also read as «wa-la taqfa», from qafa atharahu, meaning he followed his track. From the same root comes al-qafah (the trackers, experts in tracing lineage by resemblance).

﴿that of which you have no knowledge﴾: that about which your knowledge is not connected, whether through blind imitation (taqlid) or conjecture about the unseen. Those who forbid following conjecture (zann) argue from this verse. Its reply is that by knowledge ('ilm) is meant a firm belief (i'tiqad rajih) derived from an authority (sanad), whether that certainty is definite or probable. Using the word in this sense is permissible and widespread. It has also been said that the verse is restricted to matters of belief ('aqa'id). It has been said too that it refers to accusing others (ramy) and to false testimony (shahadat al-zur). This is supported by the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever accuses a believer of what is not in him, Allah will confine him in radghat al-khabal (the mire of the damned) until he brings forth an exit."

And the words of al-Kumayt:

I do not hurl accusations at the innocent without cause,
nor do I trace the chaste women if they are traced against.

﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart, all of those﴾: that is, all these organs. He treated them as rational beings, since they are asked about their states and bear witness against their owner. Although (ula'i) is mostly used for rational beings, it is the plural of dha, which covers both categories, so it has come to be used for non-rational things too, as in the line:

and life after those days.

﴿will be questioned about it﴾: in all three, the pronoun refers to each one, meaning each of them will be questioned about itself, that is, about what its owner did with it. It is also possible that the pronoun in ʿanhu refers to the verbal noun of (la taqfu), or to the owner of the hearing and sight. It has been said that the word mas'ulan is the predicate of ʿanhu, as in the verse ﴿not of those who have earned anger﴾, and the meaning would be that its owner will be asked about it. This is an error, because the agent (fa'il) and its substitute cannot precede the verb. This indicates that a servant is held accountable for his resolve to commit sin. It is also read as ﴿wal-fu'ad﴾, with the hamzah changed to a waw after a damma, and then that waw changed to a fatha.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 37–38:

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾: i.e., with exultation (marah), which is arrogance (al-ikhtiyal). It is also read "maraḥan" (as an accusative of state), and this, in terms of grammatical ruling, is more emphatic, although the verbal noun (al-masdar) is more emphatic than an explicit adjective (al-na't). ﴿Indeed, you will never tear through the earth﴾: you will never make a rent in it through the heaviness of your tread. ﴿And you will never reach the mountains in height﴾: by your self-elevation. This is a mockery of the arrogant person, and it is a justification for the prohibition, in that arrogance is pure foolishness that brings no benefit, unlike humility.

﴿All that﴾: a reference to the twenty-five traits mentioned, from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do not set up with God another god﴾. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, that these are what is written on the tablets of Moses, peace be upon him. ﴿Its evil﴾: meaning, the thing forbidden, for the things mentioned are commands and prohibitions. The two Hijazi and the two Basri readers read ﴿sayyi'uhu﴾ (its evil), taking it as the predicate of "kana" (was), with the subject being the pronoun referring to ﴿kull﴾ (all), and ﴿dhalika﴾ (that) refers specifically to what He prohibited. Accordingly, His saying ﴿hateful in the sight of your Lord﴾ is either a substitute for ﴿sayyi'uhu﴾ or an adjective of it, treated according to its sense, since it means "evil," and it has been read that way. It is also permissible for ﴿makruhan﴾ (hateful) to be in the accusative as a state (hal) of the pronoun in ﴿kana﴾, or of the adverbial phrase, on the basis that it is an adjective of ﴿sayyi'uhu﴾. What is meant by it is the hated, which is the opposite of the pleasing, not what is opposed to the willed, because of the decisive proof that all events occur by His will, Exalted is He.

"That" refers to the rulings mentioned earlier. "Of what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom" — which is knowing the truth for its own sake and the good for the sake of acting upon it. "And do not set up with Allah another god" — he repeated it to draw attention to the fact that tawhid (the oneness of God) is the beginning and the end of the matter, for whoever has no purpose behind his deed, his deed is void, and whoever intends by his action or his abstention something other than Allah, his effort is lost. It is the head of wisdom and its foundation. He related to it first what is its immediate consequence in this world, which is polytheism, and second what is its outcome in the Hereafter, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿So you will be thrown into Hell, blameworthy﴾, blaming yourself.

﴿Rejected⁠﴾: banished from the mercy of Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 40:

﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons, and taken for Himself daughters from among the angels?﴾ This is an address to those who said that the angels are the daughters of Allah. The interrogative hamza (alif-hamzah) is for denunciation, and the meaning is: Has your Lord singled you out with the best of offspring, which are sons?

﴿And has taken for Himself females from among the angels﴾, daughters for Himself. This contradicts what your intellects and your customs hold.

﴿Indeed, you utter a monstrous saying﴾ by attributing offspring to Him, which is a characteristic of some bodies, because of how quickly they pass away; then by preferring yourselves over Him, since you assign to Him what you dislike; then by making the angels, who are among the most noble of Allah's creation, the lowest of them in rank.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 17, verses 41–42**

﴿And We have certainly varied﴾ We repeated this meaning in various forms of affirmation. ﴿in this Qur'an﴾ in several passages of it. It is also possible that what is meant by "this Qur'an" is the refutation of attributing daughters to Him, on the understanding: "And We have certainly varied this statement concerning this meaning, or We have caused variation (taṣrīf) to occur in it." It was also read as "ṣaraf-nā" with the lighter pronunciation (takhfīf). ﴿so that they may take heed﴾ so that they may remember (yatadhakkarū). Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read here and in al-Furqān "li-yadhkurū," from dhikr, which has the meaning of tadhakkur (remembrance). ﴿but it only increases them in aversion﴾ from the truth, and in lack of tranquility toward it.

(Say: If there were with Him other gods, as you say) O polytheists. Ibn Kathīr and Ḥafṣ, from ʿĀṣim, read it with the yā' (third person) in this place and in what follows, on the basis that the speech is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ). Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū ʿAmr, Abū Bakr and Yaʿqūb agreed with them regarding the second instance, on the basis that the first is what the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to address to the polytheists, and the second is what He declared Himself free of by their saying.

﴿Then they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾ This is the answer to their statement and the consequent (jazāʾ) of "law" (lau, "if"). The meaning: they would have sought a way to Him who possesses dominion, by contention (muʿāzzah), as kings do with one another, or by drawing near to Him and obedience, because they know His power and their own impotence, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those whom they call upon seek the means of access to their Lord﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 43–44:

﴿Glory be to Him﴾: He is declared free of all imperfection, with complete declaring-free. ﴿And exalted above what they say, with great exaltedness﴾: He is exalted, far removed to the utmost degree from what they say. For He is at the highest level of existence, which is that He is necessary existence (wajib al-wujud) and eternal in His own essence, and taking a son is among the lowest of its levels, since it is among the attributes of things whose continuance is impossible.

﴿The seven heavens and the earth glorify Him, and whoever is in them. And there is not a thing but glorifies Him with His praise﴾: it declares Him free of what belongs to contingency (imkan) and follows from createdness (huduth), in the tongue of its state, since by their contingency and createdness they point to the eternal Creator who is necessary in His essence. ﴿But you do not understand their glorification﴾, O polytheists, because of your failure to use the correct reflection by which their glorification is understood. It is permissible to take "glorification" as a shared term between the word and the indication (al-mushtarak bayn al-lafz wal-dalala, a term that covers both verbal expression and indicative meaning), since it is attributed both to what can be conceived as uttering speech and to what cannot, and both are included according to those who permit a word to be applied to both of its meanings. Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir, Nafiʿ and Abu Bakr read "yusabbihu" with the letter ya. ﴿Indeed, He is ever Forbearing﴾, in that He did not hasten punishment upon you for your heedlessness and your polytheism. ﴿Forgiving﴾ toward whoever among you repents.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 45–46:

﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier﴾, which veils them from understanding what you recite to them.

﴿Hidden﴾: possessing a veil, like His saying, ﴿His promise is ever fulfilled﴾ (ma'tiyyan, "coming"), and their saying "a sail full (mufam)". Or it means hidden from the senses, or by another barrier. "They do not understand" and "they do not realize that they do not understand" — He negated from them the understanding of the signs revealed to them after He had negated from them the comprehension of the proofs set forth in the souls and the horizons, confirming this and clarifying that they are sealed upon misguidance, as He stated explicitly in His saying:

﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾, which conceal them and prevent them from perceiving and accepting the truth. ﴿Lest they understand it﴾, out of aversion to their understanding it. It may also be that it is an object of what is indicated by His saying, ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾, meaning: We prevented them from understanding it.

﴿And in their ears, deafness﴾, which prevents them from listening to it. Since the Qur'an is miraculous in both its wording and its meaning, He affirmed for those who deny it that which prevents understanding its meaning and perceiving its wording. ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an﴾, singular, not joined with their gods; it is a verbal noun (masdar) occupying the place of a circumstantial clause (hal), and its origin is "yahudu wahdahu", meaning "one, alone". ﴿They turn away on their backs in aversion﴾, fleeing from hearing the declaration of Divine Unity, in repulsion; or "turning away". It may also be the plural of "nafir", like "qa'id" and "qu'ud".

Al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 17, verse 47:

﴿We are most knowing of what they listen to﴾ with it, i.e., because of it, namely the mockery of you and of the Qur'an. ﴿When they listen to you﴾ is a temporal clause (zarf) governing ﴿most knowing﴾, and so is what follows. ﴿And when they are in private consultation﴾ means: We are most knowing of their purpose in listening, when they are listening to you while concealing their intent toward it, and when they are people in private consultation (najwa), conferring about it. Najwa is a verbal noun (masdar), and it may also be the plural of najiy (confidant).

﴿When the wrongdoers say: "You follow nothing but a man bewitched"﴾ is either governed by an implied "remember" (udhkur), or it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿when they are in private consultation﴾, with ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate that their private consultation with this statement is a form of wrongdoing. The "bewitched" (masḥur) is one whose magic has been worked upon him so that his reason has departed. It was also said that it means one who has sihr (magic in the sense of a physical organ), namely the lung (ri'a), i.e., "nothing but a man who breathes, eats and drinks like you."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 48–49:

﴿Behold how they coin comparisons for you.﴾ They liken you to the poet, the sorcerer, the soothsayer (kahin) and the madman. ﴿So they have gone astray﴾ from the truth in all of that. ﴿So they cannot find a way﴾ to a valid attack by which they could be consistent, so that they stumble and flounder like one bewildered in his affair, not knowing what to do, nor [do they find] a way to right guidance. ﴿And they say: "When we have become bones and crumbled particles?"﴾ meaning, debris. ﴿"Shall we indeed be resurrected in a new creation?"﴾ [This is said] in denial and disbelief, on account of the great distance and incompatibility between the softness of the living and the dryness of the decayed bones (ramim), in terms of separation and contrariness. The element governing "idha" (when) is what is indicated by "mab'uthun" (resurrected), not the word itself, because what comes after "an" (that/the particle of negation or interrogative 'an' in this construction) does not govern what precedes it. And ﴿khalqan﴾ (a creation) is either a verbal noun (masdar) or a circumstantial accusative (hal).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 50–51:

(p-258) ﴿Say﴾ in answer to them: ﴿Be stones or iron,﴾

﴿or a creation of what is greater in your breasts﴾, i.e., of what is greater in your estimation as regards acceptance of life, because it is the furthest of things from it. For His power, exalted is He, does not fall short of bringing you back to life, since bodies are alike in receiving accidents. How much more so when you are decayed bones, whereas you were once fresh and characterized by life, and the thing is more receptive to what is familiar in it than to what is not familiar. ﴿Then they will say, "Who will restore us?" Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 52:

﴿On the Day He calls you, and you will respond﴾ meaning: on the Day He resurrects you, and you will rise up. He used the metaphor of "calling" and "responding" for these two, to draw attention to their swiftness and the ease of their matter, and that the purpose of both is bringing (you) forth for reckoning and recompense. ﴿with His praise﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to them, meaning: praising Allah, exalted is He, for the perfection of His power. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 53–54:

﴿And say to My servants﴾ meaning the believers. ﴿that they should say that which is best﴾, the word that is best, and that they should not be harsh with the polytheists. ﴿Indeed, Satan incites [discord] among them﴾ he stirs up among them disputation and evil. So harshness towards them may lead to obstinacy and an increase in corruption. ﴿Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy﴾, manifest in enmity.

﴿Your Lord is most knowing of you. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you, or if He wills, He will punish you﴾ This is an explanation of ﴿that which is best﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad). That is: say to them this word and similar to it, and do not declare outright that they are among the people of the Fire, for that would incite them to evil, even though the outcome of their affair is unseen, known only to Allah. ﴿And We have not sent you over them as a guardian﴾ entrusted with their affair, to compel them to faith. Rather, We sent you only as a bringer of good news and a warner, so be gentle with them, and command your companions to bear patiently with them.

It is related that the polytheists went to excess in harming them, so they complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this was revealed.

It is also said that a man among them insulted ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), and he resolved to act against him, so Allah commanded him to pardon.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 53–54:

﴿And say to My servants﴾ meaning the believers. ﴿that they should say that which is best﴾, the word that is best, and that they should not be harsh with the polytheists. ﴿Indeed, Satan incites [discord] among them﴾ he stirs up among them disputation and evil. So harshness towards them may lead to obstinacy and an increase in corruption. ﴿Indeed, Satan is to man a clear enemy﴾, manifest in enmity.

﴿Your Lord is most knowing of you. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you, or if He wills, He will punish you﴾ This is an explanation of ﴿that which is best﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad). That is: say to them this word and similar to it, and do not declare outright that they are among the people of the Fire, for that would incite them to evil, even though the outcome of their affair is unseen, known only to Allah. ﴿And We have not sent you over them as a guardian﴾ entrusted with their affair, to compel them to faith. Rather, We sent you only as a bringer of good news and a warner, so be gentle with them, and command your companions to bear patiently with them.

It is related that the polytheists went to excess in harming them, so they complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this was revealed.

It is also said that a man among them insulted ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), and he resolved to act against him, so Allah commanded him to pardon.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 17, verse 55:

﴿Your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth.﴾ And [He knows] their states, so He chooses from among them for His prophethood and His guardianship whomever He wills. This is a rebuttal of the Quraysh's deeming it unlikely that an orphan of Abu Talib should be a prophet, and that the destitute and hungry should be his companions. ﴿And We have preferred some of the prophets over others﴾ by their soul-based virtues and their detachment from bodily attachments, not by abundance of wealth and followers, even [in the case of] Dawud, peace be upon him, for his nobility lay in what was revealed to him of the Scripture, not in the kingdom that was given to him. It is said that this is an allusion to the preferment of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). And His saying: ﴿And We gave David the Zabur (Psalms)﴾ is a reminder of the aspect of his preferment, namely that he (the Prophet ﷺ) is the Seal of the Prophets and his community is the best of communities, as indicated by what was written in the Zabur, that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants. The indefinite form of *zaburan* here, and the definite form in His saying ﴿And We have certainly written in the Zabur﴾, is because *al-zabur* is originally a passive form (*fa'ul* in the sense of *maf'ul*), like *halub* (that which is milked), or a verbal noun like *qabul*, and this is supported by the reading of Hamza with a *damma*, *al-zubur*, which is like *al-Abbas* or *al-Fadl*. Or [the indefinite is used] because the intended meaning is: We gave David some of the scriptures (*zubur*), or some portion of the Zabur, in which there is mention of the Messenger, upon him blessings and peace.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 56–57:

﴿Say: Call upon those whom you claim﴾ to be gods, ﴿besides Him﴾, such as the angels, the Messiah and ʿUzayr (Ezra). ﴿Then they have no power﴾, i.e., they are not able, ﴿to remove the harm from you﴾, such as sickness, poverty and drought, ﴿nor to change it﴾, i.e., nor can they transfer that harm from you to anyone else.

﴿Those whom they call upon themselves seek the means (wasilah) to their Lord﴾: these gods themselves seek nearness to God through obedience. ﴿Which of them is nearest﴾ is a substitution (badal) for the waw in ﴿yabtaghun﴾, meaning: he who is nearest to God among them seeks the means, so how much more so one who is not nearest. ﴿And they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment﴾, like the rest of the servants, so how can you claim that they are gods? ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is something to be feared﴾, truly deserving that everyone should beware of it, even the Messengers and the angels.

﴿And there is no town but that We will destroy it before the Day of Resurrection﴾, by death and total annihilation. ﴿Or We will punish it with a severe punishment﴾, by killing and various kinds of affliction. ﴿That was in the Book﴾, meaning in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). ﴿Inscribed﴾, meaning written.

﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs﴾, meaning: nothing turned Us away from sending the signs that Quraysh demanded. ﴿Except that the former peoples denied them﴾, meaning except the denial of the earlier generations who were similar to them in disposition, such as ʿAd and Thamud. And [this shows] that if the signs were sent, they would deny them as those [peoples] did, and would deserve annihilation according to the way (sunnah) of Our practice that has already passed. We have decreed that We will not annihilate them, because among them are those who will believe, or who will beget someone who believes. Then he mentioned some of the destroyed nations, who denied the demanded signs, so He said: ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel﴾, in response to their request. ﴿As a visible sign﴾, meaning clear, possessing sights (abṣār) or insights (baṣāʾir), or making those who saw it possessors of insight. It was also read with a fatha (mubṣiratan). ﴿But they wronged her﴾, meaning they disbelieved in her, or they wronged themselves by slaughtering her. ﴿And We do not send the signs﴾, meaning the demanded signs. ﴿Except as a warning﴾ of the descent of the total punishment; so if they do not fear, it descends. Or [it means] other than the demanded signs, such as the miracles and the verses of the Qur'an, sent only as a warning of the punishment of the Hereafter, for the matter of those to whom you were sent is deferred until the Day of Resurrection. The bāʾ (al-bāʾ, the preposition "with") here is either superfluous (zāʾidah), or it occupies the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl, a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), and the object (mafʿūl) is omitted.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 60:

﴿And [remember] when We said to you﴾ — i.e., remember when We revealed to you. ﴿Indeed your Lord has encompassed the people﴾ — so they are in the grip of His power. Or it means: He has encompassed Quraysh, in the sense of destroying them, as an enemy encompasses those he surrounds. In that case it is a good tiding of the battle of Badr, and the expression is in the past tense to affirm that it will certainly occur. ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you﴾ — [referring to] the night of the Mi'raj (the Ascension). Whoever holds that it took place in a dream is attached to this view, and whoever holds that it took place while awake interprets "vision" (ru'ya) as "sight" (ru'ya). Or [it refers to] the year of al-Hudaybiyya, when he saw that he had entered Makkah. Against this, the verse is Meccan, unless it is said that he saw it in Makkah and related it at that time. (p-260) Perhaps it was a vision he saw at the battle of Badr, based on His words, exalted is He: ﴿When God showed them to you in your dream as few﴾. It is also based on what is narrated: "When he arrived at its water he said, 'It is as if I see the places where the people will fall: this is the place where so-and-so will fall, and this is the place where so-and-so will fall.' Quraysh heard of this and mocked him."

It is said that he saw some people from the Banu Umayya climbing his pulpit and leaping upon it like monkeys, and he said, "This is their share of the world, which is given to them in return for their Islam." On this view, the meaning of His words ﴿except as a trial for the people﴾ is what happened in their days. ﴿And the accursed tree in the Qur'an﴾ is coordinated with ﴿the vision﴾, and it is the tree of al-Zaqqum. When the polytheists heard its mention, they said, "Muhammad claims that the Fire of Hell burns stones, and then says that trees grow in it." They did not know that the One who is able to protect the salamander's wool from being eaten by fire, and the entrails of the ostrich from the harm of embers and heated pieces of red-hot iron that it swallows, is able to create in the Fire a tree that the Fire does not burn. Its being cursed in the Qur'an is the cursing of those who eat from it; it is described with this figuratively for emphasis. Or [it means] that it is described as being at the root of Hell, for that is the place furthest from mercy. Or [it means] that it is hateful and harmful, from the saying "cursed food" for what is harmful. It has been interpreted as referring to Satan, Abu Jahl and al-Hakam ibn Abi al-'As. It has also been read in the nominative, as a beginning (mubtada'), with the predicate omitted, meaning: "and the accursed tree in the Qur'an is likewise."

﴿And We warn them﴾ with various kinds of warning. ﴿But it only increases them in great transgression﴾ — rebellion exceeding all bounds.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 61–62:

﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He said, "Shall I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?"﴾ [It means] "for one whom You created from clay," so it is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid). It may also be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the relative pronoun (al-rājiʿ ilā al-mawṣūl), meaning "You created him while he was clay," or [a circumstantial] from him, meaning "Shall I prostrate to him, whose origin is clay?" In all three possibilities there is an allusion to the reason for the denial.

﴿He said, "Do You see this one whom You have honored above me?"﴾ The kaf (ك) is for emphasizing the address and has no place in grammatical analysis (iʿrāb). Hādhā is the first object, and alladhī is its descriptive phrase. The second object is omitted because its relative clause indicates it. The meaning is: "Tell me about this one whom You honored over me by commanding me to prostrate to him. Why did You honor him over me?"

﴿If You delay me until the Day of Resurrection﴾ is a new sentence (kalām mubtadaʾ). The lām is a preparatory lām for the oath (lām muwaṭṭi'a li-l-qasam), and its answer is: ﴿I will surely seize his offspring, except for a few.﴾ That is, "I will uproot them through seduction, except for a few whose restraint I cannot overcome." It is derived from iḥtanaka al-jarādu al-arḍa, when locusts strip the ground of what is on it by eating, and it comes from al-ḥanak (the palate/jaw). He knew that this would be easy for him either by inference from the angels' words, ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it?﴾, together with their affirmation, or by discerning from his creation that man has delusion (wahm), desire (shahwa), and anger (ghaḍab).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 63–64:

﴿He said: "Go!"﴾ Proceed to what you intended. This is a dismissal and a leaving of him free to pursue what his soul has embellished for him. ﴿Whoever of them follows you, then indeed Hell is your recompense﴾, your recompense and theirs, so the addressee is given precedence over the absent party. It is also permissible that the address is to the followers, by way of iltifat (a shift of address). ﴿A full recompense﴾, complete, from their saying "fir li-sahibika 'irdahu" (defend your companion's honour). The accusative of jaza'an is either a masdar (verbal noun) with its verb implied, or it is governed by the sense of "tujazawna" (you will be recompensed) contained in "jaza'ukum", or it is a hal muwatti'ah (a preparatory circumstantial qualifier) for His saying "mawfuran" (full).

﴿And incite﴾, and entice. ﴿Whomever you can of them﴾ to be incited, and fazz means light, easy movement. ﴿With your voice﴾, with your call to corruption. ﴿And urge against them﴾, and shout against them, from al-jalabah, which is shouting. ﴿With your horse and your foot﴾, with your helpers, both mounted and on foot. Khayl means horsemen, and from this is his saying, peace be upon him, "O cavalry of God, mount up." Rajil is a collective noun (ism jam') for rajil (one on foot), like sahb and rakb. It is also permissible that this is a figurative image of his dominance over whoever he misleads, like a raider who cries out against a people, drives them from their places, and urges his army against them until he uproots them. Hafs recited "wa-rajilika" with a kasra, while others recited it with a damma. Both are dialects, like nadis and nadus, and its meaning is: "and gather your rajil (footmen)." It has also been read "wa-rijalika" and "wa-rijalika". ﴿And share with them in wealth﴾, by urging them to earn and gather it through the unlawful and to dispose of it in ways that are not fitting. ﴿And children﴾, by urging them to obtain offspring through a forbidden means, and associating others with him in that by naming a child 'Abd al-'Uzza, and misleading them by inducing them toward deviant creeds, base trades, and ugly deeds. ﴿And promise them﴾, false promises, such as the intercession of the gods, relying on the honour of the fathers, and postponing repentance because of long hope. ﴿And Satan promises them nothing but delusion﴾: this is a parenthetical clause explaining his false promises. Ghurur (delusion) is making error appear attractive by presenting it in a way that suggests it is correct.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 65:

﴿Indeed, My servants﴾ means the sincere ones (al-mukhlisin). The emphasis of the possessive attribution, and the restriction in His saying, ﴿except for Your servants among them, the sincere ones﴾, specifies them. ﴿You have no authority over them﴾, that is, no power over leading them astray. ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as a Trustee﴾, on whom they truly rely in seeking refuge from you.

Your Lord is the One who drives the ships for you on the sea, so that you may seek of His bounty. (Al-Baydawi:) "Yuzji" means "yujri," He causes to run. "Lakumu al-fulk fi al-bahr li-tabtaghu min fadlihi" (the ships for you on the sea, so that you may seek of His bounty): the wind and the various kinds of goods that are not with you. "Innahu kana bikum rahiman" (Indeed He is ever Merciful to you): in that He has prepared for you what you need and made easy for you what would otherwise be difficult of its means.

"Wa idha massakumu al-durr fi al-bahr" (And when harm touches you at sea): the fear of drowning. "Dalla man tad'una" (those whom you invoke vanish): everyone you invoke in your calamities departs from your thoughts. "Illa iyyahu" (except Him alone): for at that time nothing else comes to your minds, so you call upon none to remove it except Him; or it means: every one you worship has gone astray from aiding you, except Allah. "Falamma najjakum" (But when He brings you safely): from drowning. "Ila al-barri a'radtum" (to the land, you turn away): from monotheism. It has also been said: you exceeded in ingratitude for the blessing, like the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"The gift of a youth who established himself in lofty deeds... so he turned away from noble deeds and became proud."

"Wa kana al-insanu kafuran" (And man is ever ungrateful): this serves as a reason for the turning away.
