Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 68:

﴿Do you then feel secure﴾ The hamza (interrogative particle) here is for denial (inkar), and the fa' (fa, "then") is for coordination (atf) upon an omitted element whose estimate is: "Have you been saved, and so you felt secure?" That (security) led them to turn away, for the one who is able to destroy you in the sea by drowning is able to destroy you on land by sinking (the earth) and otherwise. ﴿lest He cause the side of the land to swallow you up﴾ (i.e.) lest Allah turn it over while you are upon it, or He turns it over by means of your own (sins), so "bikum" is either a circumstantial element (hal) or a complement (silah) to "yakhsifa" (lest He cause to sink). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with the nun (nun of the first person plural) in this and in the four (verses) that follow it. Mentioning "the side" is an alert that when they reached the shore they disbelieved and turned away, and that all sides and directions are equal in His power; there is no refuge in which one is safe from the causes of destruction. ﴿or send against you a violent wind (hasiban)﴾ a wind that pelts (tahsibu), i.e., throws (tarmi) with pebbles (al-hasba'), ﴿then you will not find for yourselves any protector (wakil)﴾ who will preserve you from that, for there is no one who can repel His action.

(p-262) ﴿Do you feel secure that He will not send you back into it﴾ into the sea, ﴿another time﴾ by creating winds that compel you to return and board it again.

﴿Then send upon you a violent wind (qasif) from the wind﴾ that does not pass by anything without shattering it, i.e., breaking it. ﴿And drown you﴾ — and it is narrated from Ya'qub (Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Hadrami) with the ta' (﴿فَتُغْرِقَكُمْ﴾), taking the verb as referring back to the pronoun of the wind. ﴿For what you disbelieved﴾ — because of your associating partners with Allah, or your ingratitude for the blessing of deliverance. ﴿Then you will not find for yourselves against Us any pursuer (tabi'an)﴾ — one who will follow us and seek retribution or redress.

And We have certainly honoured the Children of Adam (بَنِي آدَمَ), through the beauty of their form, the most balanced temperament, the uprightness of their stature, their distinction through reason, their ability to convey meaning through speech, gesture and writing, and their capacity for guidance (التَّهَدِّي, al-tahaddi). Or [they are honoured] through the means of livelihood and the Hereafter, their dominion over what is on the earth, their mastery of crafts, and the way that causes and effects, both higher and lower, are made to serve what benefits them, along with other things too numerous to be counted. Among these is what Ibn ʿAbbās mentioned: that every animal takes its food into its mouth, except the human being, who raises it to his mouth with his hand. ﴿And We carried them on the land and the sea﴾ on beasts and ships, from ḥamaltuhu ḥamlan (حَمَلْتُهُ حَمْلًا), meaning "I provided for him something to ride on." Or [it means] We carried them within them, so that the earth did not swallow them and the water did not drown them. ﴿And We provided them with good things﴾, namely the pleasant things, whether obtained through their own effort or without it. ﴿And We preferred them above many of those We have created, with [a certain] preference﴾, either through domination and control, or through nobility and honour. The exception is the species of angels, upon them be prayers and peace, or the elect among them. It does not follow that if the species is not preferred, none of its individuals are preferred; the matter is open to consideration. The word "many" has been interpreted as "all," but this is a strained interpretation.

**Al-Baydawi's *Anwar al-Tanzil* (Commentary) on Surah 17, verse 71:**

﴿The Day We call﴾ is in the accusative (*nusiba*). It is governed either by an implied verb, *udhkur* ("remember"), or it is an adverbial complement (*zarf*) of what is indicated by ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾. The reading *yad'u*, *yad'i* and *yad'u* was also transmitted (these are recitation variants, *qira'at*), with the alif changed to a waw, in the dialect of those who say *af'u* for *af'a* (a viper). Alternatively, the waw is a sign of the plural, as in His saying: ﴿And the wrongdoers secretly conferred﴾. Or its pronoun (the *wa* of the plural) is the subject, and *kullu* ("every") is a substitute (*badal*) for it. The final *nun* is omitted because it is little regarded, since it is only the sign of the nominative (*raf'*), and the nominative may be presumed, as in *yad'i*.

﴿every people with their leader﴾: with whomever they followed, whether a prophet, a leader in religion, a book, or a religion. It has also been said: with the book of their deeds which they had sent forward, so it will be said, "O possessor of the book of such-and-such," meaning that the bond of lineages is severed and the attribution to deeds remains. It has also been said: with the powers that carried them to their beliefs and deeds. It has also been said: with their mothers, the plural of *umm* like *khuff* and *khifaf*. The wisdom in this is to honour Jesus, peace be upon him, to show the nobility of al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, and so that the children of unlawful unions are not disgraced.

﴿Whoever is given﴾ from among those who are called. ﴿his book in his right hand﴾, that is, the book of his deeds. ﴿those will read their book﴾ joyfully and exultantly at what they see in it. ﴿and they will not be wronged a thread﴾: they will not have the least bit reduced from their rewards. The demonstrative noun (*ism al-isharah*) and the pronoun are in the plural because *man* ("whoever") is in the sense of the plural. The making of reading dependent on being given the book in the right hand indicates that whoever is given his book in his left hand, when he looks upon what is in it, will be overcome by such shame and bewilderment that they restrain his tongue from reading. For this reason He did not mention them, although His saying:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 72:

﴿And whoever is blind in this [world] will be blind in the Hereafter﴾ also indicates this, for the blind person cannot read the Book. The meaning is: whoever is blind in this worldly life, blind of heart, unable to perceive his right guidance, will be blind in the Hereafter, unable to see the path of salvation. ﴿And more astray in way﴾ than he was in this world, due to the loss of readiness (isti'dad), the lack of the instrument (alah) and the respite (muhlah). It has been said that the second is because guidance will then no longer benefit him, and "blind" is used metaphorically (mustʿar) for one who has lost a sense. It has also been said that the second [a‘mā] is a comparative (li-l-tafdil) from ʿamiya bi-qalbihi (blind in heart), like al-ajhal (more ignorant) and al-ableh (more foolish). For this reason Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub did not apply imalah to it, since the comparative form is completed by "min" (than), so its alif is treated as being in the middle (of the word) as in aʿmalikum (your deeds). This is unlike the adjectival form, whose alif falls at the end both in pronunciation and in function, so it is liable to imalah insofar as it becomes a yā' in the dual. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr applied imalah to both, while Warsh read both with an intermediate sound (bayna bayna).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 73:

﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you, so that you would fabricate against Us other than it﴾. It was revealed concerning Thaqif. They said, "We will not enter into your affair until you give us qualities by which we may boast over the Arabs: we shall not be made to pay the tithe (ushr), nor be mustered (for jihad), nor shall we be made to bow in our prayer (wa la nujba fi salatina). Whatever interest (riba) is owed to us shall be ours, and whatever interest is owed by us shall be waived from us. And that you let us enjoy al-Lat for a year, and that you make our valley sacred as you have made Makkah sacred. If the Arabs say, 'Why did you do that?' then say, 'Indeed, God commanded me.'"

It was also said that it was revealed concerning Quraysh. They said, "We will not allow you to touch the Black Stone (istilam al-hajar) until you show deference to our gods (tulimmu bi-alihatina) and touch them with your hand." Here, in (inna) is the light (mukhaffafa) form, and the lam is the distinguishing lam (lam al-fariqa). The meaning is: the matter was such that, by their insistence, they nearly caused you to fall into temptation through enticement.

﴿away from that which We revealed to you﴾, i.e., of the rulings, ﴿so that you would fabricate against Us other than it﴾, other than what We revealed to you. ﴿And then they would have taken you as a friend﴾: had you followed their desire, they would have taken you, through your being tempted, as an ally to them, having been disassociated from My guardianship.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 74–75:

﴿And had We not made you firm﴾, meaning: and had it not been for Our making you firm. ﴿You had almost inclined toward them a little﴾, meaning: you had nearly come close to following their desire. The meaning is that you were on the verge of inclining toward them, because of the strength of their deceptions and the intensity of their scheming. But Our ʿiṣmah (divine protection from error) reached you, so you were prevented from even drawing near to inclination, let alone inclining toward them. This is explicit that peace and blessings be upon him did not intend to comply with them, despite the strong motives toward it, and it is evidence that ʿiṣmah comes through God's grant of success and His preservation.

﴿Then We would have made you taste﴾, meaning: had you come close, We would have made you taste. ﴿double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death﴾, meaning: the punishment of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter, double what We punish others with in both abodes for the same act, because the error of one of great standing is more grave. The original sense of the statement was ʿadhāban ḍiʿfan fi'l-ḥayāh wa ʿadhāban ḍiʿfan fi'l-mamāt, meaning muḍāʿafan (multiplied). Then the qualified noun, الموصوف (al-mawṣūf, "the noun being described"), was deleted and the qualifier, الصفة (al-ṣifah, "the descriptive adjective"), took its place, and then it was put in the construct form as its qualified noun would be. It has been said that ḍiʿf is one of the names of punishment. It has also been said that what is meant by ﴿double of life﴾ is the punishment of the Hereafter, and ﴿double of death﴾ is the punishment of the grave. ﴿Then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us﴾, one who would repel the punishment from you.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 76–77:

﴿And if they were nearly to­ —﴾ And if the people of Makkah were nearly to [do so]. ﴿Would have driven you out﴾ would have unsettled you with their enmity. ﴿From the land﴾ the land of Makkah.

﴿To expel you from it; and then they would not remain after you﴾ If you had left, they would not remain after your departure. ﴿except a little﴾ except for a short time. This is what happened: they were destroyed at Badr, a year after his migration (hijrah). It has also been said that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews, who envied the Prophet's residence in Madinah and said: "The Levant is the place of the prophets; if you are a prophet, then go to it, so that we may believe in you." This thought occurred to his heart, so he set out a stage (marhalah), and then the verse was revealed, so he returned. Then the Banu Qurayzah were killed by him, and the Banu al-Nadir were expelled a little later. It was also read as "lā yalbathū" (with the verb in the subjunctive, نصب) governed by ﴿idhan﴾ (then), on the basis that it is coordinated with the clause of His saying ﴿And if they were nearly to, they would drive you out﴾, not on the predicate of kāda (nearly), since idhan does not govern when what follows it depends on what precedes it. Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Yaʿqub and Hafs read ﴿khilafaka﴾ (after you), and it is a dialectal form of it. The poet said:

"The dwellings became desolate after them, as though the palm-leaf weavers had spread a mat between them."

﴿The way of those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾ It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: God has established this as a custom (sunnah), namely that He destroys every nation that expelled its messenger from among its midst. The custom belongs to God, and its attribution to the messengers is because it was on their account; and this is indicated by ﴿And you will not find any change in Our way﴾, i.e., any alteration.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 78:

﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ (li-dulūk al-shams), meaning at its declining (li-zawālihā). This is indicated by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Jibril came to me at the decline of the sun (li-dulūk al-shams) when it passed its zenith, and he led me in the noon prayer (al-Ẓuhr)."

It has also been said that it means at its setting (li-ghurūbihā). The root of the word (aṣl al-tarkīb) denotes movement and transition, and from it comes al-dālik (the one rubbing), because the hand of the one rubbing does not stay still. The same applies to every combination of the letters dāl and lām, such as dalaja (to travel by night), dalaḥa, dala'a, dalafa and dalaha. It has also been said that dulūk derives from dalk (rubbing), because the one who looks at the sun rubs his eyes to ward off its rays. The lām here denotes a time limit (li-l-ta'qīt), like its use in ﴿for three nights passed﴾ (li-thalāthin khalawā). ﴿Until the darkness of the night﴾ (ilā ghasaq al-layl), meaning until its darkness, which is the time of the final night prayer (ṣalāt al-ʿishāʾ al-ākhirah). ﴿And the recitation of the dawn﴾ (wa-qur'ān al-fajr), meaning the dawn prayer (ṣalāt al-ṣubḥ). It is called "recitation" (qur'ān) because recitation is its pillar (rukn), just as it is called bowing (rukūʿ) and prostration (sujūd). It has been cited as evidence for the obligation of recitation in it, but there is no proof in it, since the figurative usage may be because it is recommended (mandūbah) in it. Yet if it is interpreted as recitation in the dawn prayer, the command to establish it indicates obligation in it explicitly, and in other prayers by analogy (qiyās). ﴿Indeed, the recitation of the dawn is ever witnessed﴾ (inna qur'āna al-fajr kāna mashhūdan), witnessed by the angels of the night and the angels of the day, or by signs of power in the change of darkness to light and of sleep, which is the brother of death, to waking, or by many of the worshippers, or by those whose right it is to witness it, the great multitude. The verse encompasses the five prayers if dulūk is interpreted as the decline, and the night prayers alone if it is interpreted as the setting. It has also been said that the intended prayer is the sunset prayer (ṣalāt al-maghrib), and His saying ﴿at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night﴾ explains the beginning and end of its time. It has been cited as evidence that the time extends until the disappearance of the twilight (ghurūb al-shafaq).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 79:

﴿And from the night, keep vigil with it﴾ and part of the night, abandon sleep for prayer. The pronoun [in "with it"] refers to the ﴿Qur'an﴾. ﴿As a supererogatory [prayer] for you﴾: an additional obligation for you beyond the obligatory prayers; or a distinction for you, because its obligation is specific to you. ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾: a station for which the one who stands in it is praised and everyone who knows of it praises him. It is unrestricted, covering every station that includes honour. The well-known view is that it is the station of intercession (shafa'ah, intercession), because of what Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: that he (ﷺ) said: "It is the station in which I will intercede for my community." And because of the indication that people will praise him for standing in it, and there is no such station except the station of intercession. Its being in the accusative as an adverb of place is by implying its verb, meaning "so He will establish you in a station," or by taking ﴿yab'athaka﴾ to include its meaning; or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state, meaning "that He will raise you as one possessing a station."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 80–81:

﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to enter"﴾, meaning into the grave. ﴿an entry of truthfulness﴾, meaning an entry that is pleasing. ﴿And cause me to exit﴾, meaning from it at the Resurrection.

﴿an exit of truthfulness﴾, meaning an exit accompanied by honour. It was also said that the intended meaning is entering Medina and exiting Mecca. It was said that it means entering Mecca in a state of triumph over it and exiting it safe from the polytheists. It was said that it means entering the cave and exiting it safe. It was said that it means entering upon the burdens of the Message that he bore and exiting from them having fulfilled its duty. It was said that it means entering into everything he is involved with, whether a place or a matter, and exiting from it.

It was also recited as "madkhala" and "makhraja" with a fatha, meaning: "He caused me to enter, so I entered an entry, and He caused me to exit, so I exited an exit." ﴿And grant me from Yourself an authority to help me﴾, meaning a proof that supports me against those who oppose me, or a ruler who supports Islam against disbelief. So He answered him with His words: ﴿Indeed, the party of Allah, they are the victorious﴾, ﴿that He may make it prevail over all religion﴾, ﴿He will surely grant them succession upon the earth﴾.

﴿And say, "The truth has come"﴾, meaning Islam, ﴿and falsehood has vanished﴾, meaning it has gone away and perished, and shirk has perished. The word is from "zahaqa rūhuhu," meaning his soul departed when it left. ﴿Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾ (p-265), meaning dissolving and not lasting. On the authority of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, entered Mecca on the day of the Conquest, and in it there were three hundred and sixty idols. He would poke at the eye of each one of them with his mikhsarah (a short staff) and say, "The truth has come and falsehood has vanished," and each one would fall on its face, until he had cast down all of them. The idol of Khuza'ah remained atop the Ka'bah, and it was of brass. He said, "O Ali, throw it down," so he climbed up and threw it down, and it broke.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 82:

﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers﴾. It is, for the rectification of their religion and the reform of their souls, like the healing medicine for the sick. The ﴿min﴾ (from/of) here is explicative (li-l-bayan), for all of it is like this. It was also said that it is partitive (li-l-tab'idh), and the meaning is that among it is that which heals from illness, such as al-Fatiha and the verses of healing. The two Basrans read ﴿nunazzilu﴾ (We send down) with light (takhfif) pronunciation. ﴿And it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾, due to their denial and their disbelief in it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 83–84:

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man﴾, with health and abundance, he turns away from the remembrance of Allah. ﴿And turns aside with his side﴾: he twists his side away and distances himself from it, as if he were self-sufficient and independent in his affairs. It is also permissible that this is a metaphor (kinaya) for arrogance, since it is the custom of the arrogant. Ibn ʿAmir, in the narration of Ibn Dhakwan, read here and in "Fussilat" (wa-nāʾin) on the pattern of metathesis (qalb), or because it means "rose up" (nahada). ﴿And when evil touches him﴾, from illness or poverty, ﴿he is despairing﴾: intensely despairing of the mercy of Allah.

﴿Say: Each acts according to his manner (shakilatihi)﴾. Say: every person acts according to his way that conforms to his state in guidance and misguidance, or according to the essence of his soul and his dispositions that follow the temperament of his body. ﴿Your Lord knows best who is best guided in the way﴾: whose path is most upright and whose method is clearest. The shakila has been explained as nature, custom, and religion.

They ask you about the **spirit** (*al-rūḥ*), which is that by which the human body is given life and is governed. Say: **"The spirit is of the affair of my Lord"** (﴿قُلِ الرُّوحُ مِن أمْرِ رَبِّي﴾). It is among the originated things (*al-ibdā'iyyāt*) that come into being by "Be" (*kun*) without matter, and it is not generated from a root like the organs of the body. Or it means that it was brought into existence by His command and came about by His bringing-into-being, so that the question concerns whether it is eternal or originated. It was also said that it is among the things whose knowledge God has kept to Himself. This is based on what has been narrated: "The Jews said to the Quraysh, 'Ask him about the People of the Cave, about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and about the spirit. If he answers them or remains silent, he is not a prophet; but if he answers some and remains silent about others, then he is a prophet.' So he explained the two stories to them and left the matter of the spirit unspecified, and it is unspecified in the Torah."

It was also said that the spirit is Gabriel, or that it is a creation greater than the angel, or that it is the Qur'an, and "of the affair of my Lord" means "of His revelation." **"And you have been given of knowledge only a little"** (﴿وَما أُوتِيتُمْ مِنَ العِلْمِ إلا قَلِيلا﴾): you acquire it through the mediation of your senses, for the intellect's acquisition of theoretical knowledge (*al-maʿārif al-naẓariyya*) is derived only from necessary knowledge (*al-ḍarūriyyāt*) which is obtained through the sense perception of particulars (*juzʾiyyāt*). That is why it is said: whoever lacks a sense has lacked a branch of knowledge. Perhaps most things are not perceived by the senses, nor is any of their known states perceived in themselves. This is an indication that the spirit is among those things whose essence cannot be known except through accidents that distinguish it from what is mixed with it. Therefore He limited the answer to this, just as Moses limited his answer to Pharaoh's question, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?" (﴿وما رَبُّ العالَمِينَ﴾), by mentioning some of His attributes.

It is narrated that when (ﷺ) said this to them, they said, "Are we specifically addressed by this statement?" He said, "No, rather we and you." They said, "How wondrous is your matter! At one moment you say, **'Whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good'** (﴿وَمَن يُؤْتَ الحِكْمَةَ فَقَدْ أُوتِيَ خَيْرًا كَثِيرًا﴾), and at another moment you say this." Then it was revealed: **"And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens..."** (﴿وَلَوْ أنَّما في الأرْضِ مِن شَجَرَةٍ أقْلامٌ﴾). What they said was due to their misunderstanding, because human wisdom is that one knows of good and truth what human capacity can contain, indeed what ensures the good of his livelihood and his hereafter. Compared with God's knowledge, which has no end, this is little, by which one attains the good of both abodes; yet compared with it, it is much.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 86–87:

﴿And if We willed, We would surely take away that which We have revealed to you﴾. The first lam (lam al-tawtia, the preparatory lam) prepares for an oath (qasam), and ﴿surely take away﴾ (la-nadhhabanna) is its answer, which takes the place of the answer to the conditional clause (jaza' al-shart). The meaning is: if We willed, We would take away the Qur'an and erase it from the codices (al-masahif) and from the breasts (al-sudur), ﴿then you would not find for yourself any guardian (wakil) against Us in regard to it﴾, that is, anyone who would undertake, against Us, its recovery (istirdad) as something inscribed (masturan) and preserved (mahfuzan).

﴿Except as a mercy from your Lord﴾. For if it reaches you, then perhaps it will be restored to you. It is also permissible that this be an exceptive clause of the disconnected type (istithna' munqati'), with the sense of "but rather, a mercy from your Lord has left it [in place], not taken away." In that case it is a favor (imtinan) by its preservation after the blessing of its revelation (minnah fi tanzilihi). ﴿Indeed, His bounty toward you has been great﴾, such as His sending you [as a messenger], His sending down the Book upon you, and His preserving it in His protection.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 88–89:

﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an﴾ in eloquence, excellence of arrangement and perfection of meaning. ﴿they would not produce its like﴾, even though among them are the pure Arabs (al-'arab al-'ariba), the masters of rhetoric (arbab al-bayan) and the people of verification (ahl al-tahqiq). This is the answer to an omitted oath, indicated by the preceding lam (al-lam al-muwatti'a, the lam of preparation), for were it not for it, the answer of the conditional would be unjussified (bila jazm), because the conditional is in the past tense, as in the verse of Zuhayr:

"And if a close friend comes to him on the day of request, he says: 'My wealth is not absent, nor is there a sacred prohibition.'"

﴿And even if some of them were to be aids to others﴾ even if they backed one another in attempting to bring its like. Perhaps he did not mention the angels because their bringing its like would not remove it from being a miracle, and because they were intermediaries in bringing it. It is also possible that this verse is a confirmation of His words: ﴿Then you would not find for yourself any advocate against Us in regard to it﴾.

﴿And We have certainly diversified﴾ We have repeated [it] in various ways, for greater affirmation and clarification. ﴿for mankind in this Qur'an from every example﴾ from every meaning which is like an example in its strangeness and in its striking the souls in the right place. ﴿But most of the people refused except disbelief﴾ except denial. That this construction is permissible, while "I struck none except Zayd" is not, is because [the phrase here] is interpreted as containing a negation.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 90–91:

﴿And they say: "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth"﴾ — out of obstinacy and by way of demanding proposals, after the proof had already been established against them through the clarification of the inimitability of the Qur'an and the joining to it of other miracles.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 17, verses 92–93:

﴿Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed﴾ (meaning) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or We cause pieces of the sky to fall upon them﴾. The word *kisafan* (pieces) is like *qita'* (fragments) in both wording and meaning. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it with a sukun (*sakkanahu*, i.e., without a vowel on the *sin*) throughout the Qur'an, except in al-Rum (p-267). Ibn 'Amir reads it that way except in this surah. Abu Bakr and Nafi' read it that way in other places, and Hafs does so except in al-Tur. It is either a lightened form of the vowelled *kisafan*, as in *sidratin* and *sidrin* (lote-tree and lote-trees), or a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, as in *al-tahn* (the ground grain, i.e., "that which is ground"). ﴿Or you bring God and the angels as a guarantor (*qabilan*)﴾ as a surety for what you claim, meaning a witness to its truth and a guarantor for its consequences; or *qabilan* means "facing/confronting," like *al-'asheer* in the sense of "companion," and it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to God, while the circumstantial clause for the angels is omitted because it is indicated by the first, as the predicate is omitted in the saying of the poet:

"Indeed I and Qayyar therein are strangers"

Or it means a group, in which case it is a circumstantial clause referring to the angels.

﴿Or you have a house of gold (*zukhruf*)﴾ made of gold; it has been read that way, and its original meaning is adornment. ﴿Or you ascend into the sky﴾ through its ascending paths. ﴿And we will not believe in your ascent﴾ alone ﴿until you bring down to us a book that we may read﴾ in which there is your confirmation. ﴿Say: Glory be to my Lord﴾, in wonder at their proposals, or to exalt God above coming, or above being subject to any command, or above anyone sharing with Him in power. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read: "He said, Glory be to my Lord," meaning the Messenger said: ﴿Am I anything but a human being, a messenger?﴾ like the rest of mankind and like the other messengers. They did not bring their peoples anything except what God manifested to them, in accordance with the condition of their peoples. The matter of signs was not up to them, nor were they entitled to dictate to God, so that you would choose them over me. This is the general answer, and the detailed answer has been mentioned in other verses, such as His saying: ﴿And if We had sent down to you a book on paper﴾, and ﴿And if We had opened a gate for them﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 94–95:

﴿And what prevented the people from believing when the guidance came to them﴾, i.e., what prevented them from faith after the revelation had descended and the truth had become manifest.

﴿Except that they said: "Has Allah sent a mere human as a messenger?"﴾ Except their this statement. The meaning is that no doubt remained for them that would prevent them from believing in Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an, except their denial that Allah should send a human.

﴿Say﴾ in answer to their doubt: ﴿"Had there been in the earth angels walking"﴾ as the children of Adam walk, ﴿"at rest"﴾ dwelling in it, ﴿"We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger."﴾ Because they would be able to meet him and receive from him, whereas humankind, most of them are blind to perceiving an angel and receiving from him, for that is conditioned upon a kind of affinity and similarity. And "malakan" (an angel) may be a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of "rasūlan" (a messenger), and it may be a descriptive modifier of it; likewise "basharan" (a human). The first (the circumstantial reading) is more fitting.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 96:

﴿Say: "Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you."﴾ As to my being the Messenger of Allah to you, by His manifesting the miracle in accordance with my claim; or as to my having conveyed what I was sent with to you, and your having opposed me. "Shahidan" (as a witness) is in the accusative, either as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) or as a specification (tamyiz). ﴿Indeed, He is ever, of His servants, All-Aware, All-Seeing.﴾ He knows their inner and outer states and will recompense them for them. In this there is consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) and a warning to the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 97–98:

﴿And whomever Allah guides, he is the one guided; and whomever He leads astray, you will not find for them allies besides Him.﴾ [They will guide him.] ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces.﴾ [They will be dragged upon them, or they will walk upon them.]

It was narrated that it was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How will they walk upon their faces?" He said: "Indeed, the One who made them walk upon their feet is capable of making them walk upon their faces." ﴿Blind, dumb and deaf.﴾ They will not see what would delight their eyes, nor hear what would be pleasing to their ears, nor speak in a way that would be accepted from them, because in their worldly life they did not seek insight through the signs and lessons, and they turned deaf ears to hearing the truth, and refused to speak the truth. It is also permissible that they will be gathered, after the reckoning, from the place of standing to (p-268) the Fire, with their faculties and senses impaired. ﴿Their refuge is Hell; whenever its flame subsides﴾ its blaze dies down, by consuming their skins and flesh. ﴿We increase for them the blaze﴾ its intensity, by replacing their skins and flesh so that they return blazing and flaming. It is as if, since they denied the return after annihilation, Allah requites them by making them continually subject to return and annihilation, and to this He alluded with His words:

﴿That is their recompense, because they disbelieved in Our signs and said, "When we have become bones and crumbled remains, will we indeed be resurrected in a new creation?"﴾ Because the reference is to the punishment of them that preceded.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 99–100:

﴿Have they not seen﴾ — or: have they not known — ﴿that God, who created the heavens and the earth, is able to create the likes of them﴾? For they are not stronger in creation than they, and restoration is not harder for Him than the first beginning. ﴿And He has appointed for them a term about which there is no doubt﴾: it is death or the Resurrection. ﴿But the wrongdoers refused﴾, despite the clarity of the truth, ﴿except to deny﴾, except to reject stubbornly.

﴿Say: Even if you possessed the treasuries of the mercy of my Lord﴾ — the treasuries of His provision and all His bounties — and "you" is the subject of a verb whose meaning is explained by what follows it, like the saying of Hatim:

*Had it been a woman with bracelets who slapped me...*

The purpose of this omission and explanation is emphasis together with brevity, and an indication of exclusivity. ﴿Then you would surely withhold, for fear of spending﴾ — you would be stingy, for fear of exhaustion through spending, since there is no one who does not prefer benefit for himself; and even if he gives something to another, he gives it only for a return that exceeds it. So he is, in that case, stingy compared with the generosity and munificence of God Most High. Moreover, stingy people are the majority among them. ﴿And man has always been niggardly﴾ — stingy, because his affairs are built upon need, upon holding back what he requires, and upon watching for a return on what he gives.

﴿And We certainly gave Moses nine clear signs﴾: they are the staff, the hand, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the water gushing from the stone, the splitting of the sea, and the lifting of the mountain over the Children of Israel. It is also said they were the flood, the years of drought, and the loss of crops in place of the last three.

It is narrated from Safwan that a Jew asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about them, and he said: "That you do not associate anything with God, do not steal, do not commit adultery, do not kill the soul which God has forbidden except by right, do not practice sorcery, do not consume usury, do not walk with an innocent person to a ruler so that he may kill him, do not slander a chaste woman, and do not flee from the battlefield. And especially for you Jews: do not transgress on the Sabbath." So the Jew kissed his hand and his foot.

According to this, the meaning of "signs" is the general rulings common to the religious communities (milal), which are established in all the revealed laws (sharā'i', plural of sharī'a, divine law). They were called signs because they indicate the state of whoever engages with their subject matter in the Hereafter, whether happiness or misery.

His statement "and especially for you Jews: do not transgress" is a separate, additional ruling beyond the answer, and for this reason the structure of the speech was changed.

﴿So ask the Children of Israel when he came to them﴾. We said to him: ask them about Pharaoh, so that he would send them with you; or ask them about the state of their religion. This is supported by the recitation (qirā'a) of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), "fa-sa'ala" (so he asked), in the past tense without a hamza, which is the dialect of Quraysh. The word *idh* (when) is connected either to *qulnā* (We said) or to *sa'ala* (he asked) according to this recitation, or, O Muhammad, ask the Children of Israel about what took place between Moses and Pharaoh when he came to them; or about the signs, so that the truth of your message becomes evident to the polytheists, or so that your soul is consoled; or so that you know that if God had brought them what they proposed, they would have persisted in obstinacy and arrogance like those before them; or so that your certainty increases, because the accumulation of proofs produces strength of certainty and tranquillity of heart. On this view, *idh* is in the accusative governed by *ātaynā* (We gave), or by an implied *yukhbirūka* (they will inform you), in which case it is the answer to the imperative, or by an implied *udhkur* (remember), as a resumption. ﴿Pharaoh said to him: "I truly think you, O Moses, are bewitched"﴾: you have been bewitched, so your mind has become confused.(p-269)

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 102:**

﴿He said: "Indeed you know"﴾, O Pharaoh. Al-Kisa'i (d. 189 AH) read it with a damma (*ʿalā ikhbārihi ʿan nafsihi*), as a report of the speaker about himself. ﴿"That none has sent these down"﴾, meaning the signs. ﴿"Except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear evidences (*baṣāʾir*)"﴾, clear proofs that make you perceive my truthfulness, but you are obstinate. Its being in the accusative is as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*, a term for an accusative describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). ﴿"And indeed I think you, O Pharaoh, to be ruined (*mathbūran*)"﴾, turned away from good, stamped upon evil, from their saying: *mā thabarak ʿan hādhā*, meaning "what turned you away from this?" Or: destroyed. He opposed his assumption with his own assumption. There is a vast difference between the two assumptions: Pharaoh's assumption is pure falsehood, while Moses' assumption hovers around certainty, given the manifest signs of it. It is also recited as: ﴿"And indeed I think you, O Pharaoh, to be utterly ruined (*la-mathbūran*)"﴾, with *in* being the lightened (*mukhaffafa*) form and the *lām* being the distinguishing *lām* (*al-lām al-fāriqa*).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 103–104:

﴿So he intended﴾ Pharaoh. ﴿To drive them out﴾ to make Musa and his people light (of foot) and to expel them. ﴿From the land﴾ the land of Egypt, or the land in general, by killing and uprooting.

﴿So We drowned him and those with him, all of them﴾ We turned his scheme back upon him, and We made him and his people light (of foot) by drowning them.

﴿And We said after him﴾ after Pharaoh, or after his drowning, ﴿to the Children of Israel: "Dwell in the land﴾ which he intended to drive you out of. ﴿And when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾ the (second) turn, or the life, or the Hour, or the Hereafter, meaning the Resurrection. ﴿We will bring you forth in a mixed multitude﴾ mingled together, you and them. Then We will judge between you and distinguish your happy ones from your wretched ones. Al-lafif (لَفِيفًا) means groups from various tribes.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 103–104:

﴿So he intended﴾ Pharaoh. ﴿To drive them out﴾ to make Musa and his people light (of foot) and to expel them. ﴿From the land﴾ the land of Egypt, or the land in general, by killing and uprooting.

﴿So We drowned him and those with him, all of them﴾ We turned his scheme back upon him, and We made him and his people light (of foot) by drowning them.

﴿And We said after him﴾ after Pharaoh, or after his drowning, ﴿to the Children of Israel: "Dwell in the land﴾ which he intended to drive you out of. ﴿And when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾ the (second) turn, or the life, or the Hour, or the Hereafter, meaning the Resurrection. ﴿We will bring you forth in a mixed multitude﴾ mingled together, you and them. Then We will judge between you and distinguish your happy ones from your wretched ones. Al-lafif (لَفِيفًا) means groups from various tribes.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 105–106:

﴿And with the truth We sent it down, and with the truth it descended﴾. That is: We did not send down the Qur'an except as being joined with the truth that required its sending down, and it did not descend upon the Messenger except as being joined with the truth that it comprised. It has been said: We did not send it down from the heaven except as guarded by the watch of the angels, and it did not descend upon the Messenger except as guarded by them from the mixing of the devils. Perhaps he intended by this the negation of falsehood affecting it at the beginning and at the end. ﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good news﴾ to the obedient, of reward, ﴿and a warner﴾ to the disobedient, of punishment. So there is nothing upon you except conveying good news and warning.

﴿And a Qur'an We have separated﴾: We sent it down in parts, distributed over time. It has been said: We distinguished within it the truth from falsehood, and the preposition was omitted, as in His saying: "and a day We witnessed it" (fa-hudhf al-jarr). It was also read with the doubled letter (tashdid, fa-farraqnahu) because of the abundance of its installments, for it descended over the course of some twenty years. ﴿So that you might recite it to the people at a pause﴾: at leisure and with deliberation, for that is easier for memorization and more helpful for understanding. It was also read with a fatha on the mim (ʿalā makthin, makath), and that is a dialect of the same word. ﴿And We have sent it down in stages﴾: according to the occurrence of events.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verses 108–109:

﴿And they say, "Glory be to our Lord!"﴾ — exalting Him above the failure to keep a promise. ﴿Indeed the promise of our Lord was bound to be fulfilled.﴾ — that is, His promise was certain to come to pass, without doubt.

﴿And they fall down upon their faces, weeping﴾ — He repeated it because the state and the cause differ: the first (prostration) is for gratitude upon the fulfilment of the promise, and the second is for what the admonitions of the Qur'an have impressed upon them, while they weep out of fear of God. He mentioned the chin (dhqan, "chin") because it is the first part of the face of the one prostrating that touches the ground, and the lam in (li-l-adhqan) indicates that the falling down is specific to it. ﴿And it increases them﴾ — the hearing of the Qur'an increases them in humility (khushu'), just as it increases them in knowledge and certainty concerning God.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 110:

﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful (al-Rahman). Whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ It was revealed when the polytheists heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saying: "O Allah, O Merciful (Ya Rahman)." They said: "He forbids us to worship two gods, yet he calls upon another god." Or it was said that the Jews said: "You make little mention of the Merciful, whereas Allah has mentioned Him abundantly in the Torah." The meaning according to the first reading is the equivalence between the two names, in that both are applied to one essence, although the consideration in applying each of them differs; and the unity (of reference) is only for the Essence who is the absolute object of worship. According to the second reading, the two are equal in the goodness of their application and in leading to the intended purpose, and this is the better reading, due to His saying: ﴿Whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ The "calling" (du'a') in the verse means "naming," and it is transitive to two objects, the first of which has been omitted as being understood. The "or" (aw) is for choice. The tanwin in ﴿ayyan﴾ is a substitute for the genitive complement; and ﴿ma﴾ is a supplementary particle to emphasize the indefiniteness contained in ﴿ayyan﴾. The pronoun in ﴿falahu﴾ refers to the named (al-musamma), because the naming belongs to Him, not to the name. The original structure of the sentence would have been ﴿whichever you call﴾, and it is good; it was placed in its position as ﴿falahu al-asma' al-husna﴾ for emphasis and to indicate what the evidence points to. That they are "most beautiful" is due to their indicating attributes of majesty and generosity. ﴿And do not speak your prayer aloud﴾ by reciting your prayer loudly until you make the polytheists hear, for that would lead them to revile and speak idly during it. ﴿Nor be silent in it﴾ so that you do not make those behind you among the believers hear. ﴿And seek a way between those﴾ between loudness and silence. ﴿A way﴾ moderate, for moderation in all matters is loved.

It is narrated that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) used to recite quietly, saying: "I confide in my Lord, and He knows my need." And Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) used to recite loudly, saying: "I drive away the Shaytan and awaken the drowsy." So when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded Abu Bakr to raise his voice a little, and Umar to lower his voice a little.

It was also said that its meaning is: do not recite aloud your entire prayer, nor be entirely silent in it, but seek a way between those, by reciting quietly by day and aloud by night.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 17, verse 111:

﴿And say: "All praise is due to Allah, who has not taken a son, and has no partner in dominion"﴾ in divinity. ﴿"and has no protector out of humiliation"﴾: no ally who befriends Him out of a humiliation befalling Him, so that he might ward it off through that alliance. By this it is negated that He has anything that shares His kind or is of another kind, whether by choice or by necessity, or anything that assists Him and strengthens Him. He tied praise to this to indicate that He is the One who deserves all kinds of praise, because He is perfect in His essence, uniquely responsible for existence, and bestows blessings absolutely, whereas everything else is deficient, a possession of a blessing, or one upon whom a blessing is bestowed. For this reason His saying is joined to it: ﴿"And magnify Him with magnification"﴾. In this there is a reminder that the servant, however much he exceeds in tanzih (declaring God free from every imperfection) and tamjid (glorifying Him), and however hard he strives in worship and praise, should acknowledge his shortfall in fulfilling his duty in that regard.

(p-271) It is narrated that "whenever a boy of the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib became eloquent, the Prophet (ﷺ) would teach him this verse." And from him, peace be upon him: "Whoever recites Surat Bani Isra'il and his heart softens at the mention of the two parents, he will have a qintar in Paradise." A qintar is one thousand uqiyyah and two hundred uqiyyah. And Allah knows best the correct understanding, and to Him is the return and the final resort.
